verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at any level. The patch deletes four functions with no callers in core, and two committers who know heaptuple.c proposed and backed the removal in messages #1 to #3. The only cost is that an out-of-tree caller fails to build against the new major version, which is how Postgres normally removes C API. Confidence is medium because only three of six messages are visible and the code was not read.

brief.title: Remove unused heap_expand_tuple(), minimal_expand_tuple() and related functions

brief.proposed_design: The patch deletes the four functions from heaptuple.c and their declarations from htup_details.h. It also rewords two comments in the fast_default regression test that name expand_tuple(), so they refer to the code that now handles missing attributes.

precedents_retrieved.title: Removing unused trailing linepointers from heap pages
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch truncates unused line pointers at the end of a heap page's line pointer array, which lowers pd_lower and returns that space for tuple data. Later versions also did this truncation during pruning, beyond the VACUUM-only truncation added in Postgres 14.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Geoghegan asked for concrete evidence before the patch could be committed: a benchmark or test showing a measurable benefit, such as smaller on-disk table size, or at least no regressions. That request went unanswered and the thread stalled, so the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I just want to see
some concrete testing, maybe with pgbench, or with an artificial test
case.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove unused #include's
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andres Freund, Álvaro Herrera, Tom Lane, Nathan Bossart
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes #include lines that clangd, and later include-what-you-use, reported as unused. It started with src/backend/commands and then grew to cover all of src/.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch after senior reviewers objected. Several removals broke builds under other platforms or options, and some removed headers were still included through other headers, so the source did not improve. Tom Lane said past bad experiences with automated #include removal make developers wary of work that may need undoing, and Nathan Bossart did not want hundreds of small cleanup commits.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The currently available tools are probably smarter
than what we were using back then, but they're evidently still not
perfect, and we're leery of having to undo work.

precedents_retrieved.title: Simplify ExecWithoutOverlapsNotEmpty by removing unused parameter
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the unused atttypid parameter from the static function ExecWithoutOverlapsNotEmpty(). It also replaces a lookup_type_cache() call, made only to read typtype, with get_typtype().
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Two reviewers approved the patch, and Chao Li noted that get_typtype() returns '\0' instead of raising an error for an invalid type OID, which changes the error message. No message shows the author answering or withdrawing the patch.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove unused function parameters, part 1: contrib
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set removes unused function parameters across contrib modules, split per module and found with a coccinelle script. For citext, v1 made internal_citext_pattern_cmp() use its unused collid argument, and v2 removed the argument.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Reviewers built and tested the patches and Jacob Champion found v2-0005 more correct, with no objection raised. The thread ends on 2025-12-01, and the entry was withdrawn on 2026-02-13 with no message explaining it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Expand applicability of aggregate's sortop optimization
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner keep the index-based MIN/MAX optimization for aggregates with an ORDER BY clause, such as MIN(x ORDER BY x), when the ordering uses the same column and a sort operator from the same btree opfamily as the aggregate's sortop. Later in the thread, Andrei Lepikhov reworked it into an aggregate support function (prosupport) that removes the aggregate's ORDER BY for min/max.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane reviewed the prosupport version and found no documentation for the new support request. He doubted that sharing a btree opfamily justifies removing the ORDER BY clause, given opposite sort directions and plans without an index. He also found no check that the aggregated and ordering expressions match, and questioned whether MIN(x ORDER BY x) occurs often enough to be worth the planning cycles. The original author then closed the entry because the patch had become a different patch, and suggested a new entry for it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Also, I am far from convinced that the code is right: the fact that the aggsortop shares a btree opfamily with orderClause->sortop doesn't seem to be enough to justify removing the aggorder clause.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove unused function parameters, part 2: replication
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andres Freund, Amit Kapila, Daniel Gustafsson
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes unused parameters from static functions in src/backend/replication, such as ReorderBufferRestoreCleanup(), ApplyLogicalMappingFile() and apply_handle_origin(). A coccinelle script found the parameters.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund saw little gain and said several parameters are intentional: the ReorderBuffer arguments and the relid in ApplyLogicalMappingFile() keep the API consistent with nearby functions. Amit Kapila wanted to keep the RetainDeadTuplesData and StringInfo arguments for consistency with related functions and possible future use. Michael Paquier and Daniel Gustafsson said removal pays off only when it simplifies callers, for example by not opening a Relation, and otherwise costs backpatch conflicts. The author asked for guidance and later withdrew the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
They intentionally get the reorderbuffer,
it's an implementation detail that the *txn argument happens to currently be
sufficient.

precedents_retrieved.title: partial heap only tuples
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds partial heap only tuples (PHOT), so an update creates new index tuples only for indexes whose columns changed, and those index tuples point to the new heap tuple. Index scans follow a PHOT chain only while their own indexed columns stay unchanged, and pruning of PHOT chains is restricted.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stopped applying to HEAD, and the entry was set to Waiting for Author in July 2021. No updated patch was posted, so the entry was returned with feedback in November 2021. The visible messages show design concerns, such as index create/drop handling and long-term heap fragmentation, but no objection that decided the outcome.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: As no update has been posted, the patch still doesn't apply.

precedents_retrieved.title: Expand the use of check_canonical_path() for more GUCs
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch applied check_canonical_path() to more path GUCs: promote_trigger_file, krb_server_keyfile and the ssl_* file settings. It also added comments in guc.c explaining why data_directory, config_file, hba_file and ident_file already get canonicalized at postmaster startup.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut questioned why any GUC needs check_canonical_path(); he found the remaining calls in guc.c were leftovers from when data_directory and config_file were canonicalized there, and noted that canonicalize_path() does not make relative paths absolute. Tom Lane said user-given strings should not be altered without need, and that canonicalization matters only where other paths are derived from the value. The author concluded there was consensus to perhaps remove some canonicalization but not to expand it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Yes, that's fair as there is visibly a consensus that we could perhaps
remove some of the canonicalization, but not expand it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Optimize order of GROUP BY keys".
Reverted commit(s): Optimize order of GROUP BY keys
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit db0d67db2401eb6238ccc04c6407a4fd4f985832 and
several follow-on fixes.  The idea of making a cost-based choice
of the order of the sorting columns is not fundamentally unsound,
but it requires cost information and data statistics that we don't
really have.  For example, relying on procost to distinguish the
relative costs of different sort comparators is pretty pointless
so long as most such comparator functions are labeled with cost 1.0.
Moreover, estimating the number of comparisons done by Quicksort
requires more than just an estimate of the number of distinct values
in the input: you also need some idea of the sizes of the larger
groups, if you want an estimate that's good to better than a factor of
three or so.  That's data that's often unknown or not very reliable.
Worse, to arrive at estimates of the number of calls made to the
lower-order-column comparison functions, the code needs to make
estimates of the numbers of distinct values of multiple columns,
which are necessarily even less trustworthy than per-column stats.
Even if all the inputs are perfectly reliable, the cost algorithm
as-implemented cannot offer useful information about how to order
sorting columns beyond the point at which the average group size
is estimated to drop to 1.

Close inspection of the code added by db0d67db2 shows that there
are also multiple small bugs.  These could have been fixed, but
there's not much point if we don't trust the estimates to be
accurate in-principle.

Finally, the changes in cost_sort's behavior made for very large
changes (often a factor of 2 or so) in the cost estimates for all
sorting operations, not only those for multi-column GROUP BY.
That naturally changes plan choices in many situations, and there's
precious little evidence to show that the changes are for the better.
Given the above doubts about whether the new estimates are really
trustworthy, it's hard to summon much confidence that these changes
are better on the average.

Since we're hard up against the release deadline for v15, let's
revert these changes for now.  We can always try again later.

Note: in v15, I left T_PathKeyInfo in place in nodes.h even though
it's unreferenced.  Removing it would be an ABI break, and it seems
a bit late in the release cycle for that.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent in the list matches this proposal or gives a reason that applies to it. [P22], [P12] and [P16] were dead-code removals, but none records why it was not accepted. [P6] stalled on unused parameters kept for API consistency and on backpatch conflicts; neither concern applies to deleting whole uncalled functions. In the thread, Tom Lane gave +1 (message #2) and Kyle Snavely found no issues (message #5). Not checked: which external code was searched for callers (message #1).

Nothing in the user-facing contract changes: no SQL, GUC, catalog, pg_dump or psql surface. The only compatibility effect is removing three exported C functions in a major release, which Postgres does routinely; an extension that calls them fails loudly at build or load time, not silently. Tom Lane agreed in message #2. [P6] does not apply because its concern was churn in code that is still used.

The patch creates no persistent or cross-node state, so this angle finds no objection. It removes C functions with no callers from master only, and changes no on-disk tuple format, WAL record, catalog, or wire protocol message. Fast-default tuples on disk are still read by the code that handles missing attributes today. Dropping exported functions in a new major release is normal practice, Andres Freund found no external callers, and Tom Lane agreed in message #2.

The patch only deletes unused C functions from heaptuple.c and htup_details.h and rewords two test comments. It adds no privilege, SQL-callable surface, GUC, catalog entry or new data exposure, so there is no security or privilege aspect to object to.

From the maintenance angle this patch lowers the long-run cost, since it deletes about 250 lines of nontrivial tuple-expansion code that nothing in core calls. Two committers who know heaptuple.c, Andres Freund and Tom Lane, proposed and backed it in messages #1 to #3. A third-party extension that still calls these functions would fail to build against the new major version, which is the usual way Postgres removes C API in a major release. Andres Freund searched for external callers and found none (message #1), though the thread does not say what code he searched. The objection recorded in [P6], backpatch conflicts for little gain, does not apply here. The functions are removed whole, so a fix to them on a back branch has nothing to merge into in master.

This angle has nothing to raise. The proposal adds no feature that an existing mechanism or extension could cover; it removes four functions with no core callers. Any concern about out-of-core callers belongs to a compatibility angle, not this one.

The demand angle does not fit a removal of dead code: the patch adds no feature that needs users, and it lowers maintenance cost for everyone. Two committers who know the area proposed or backed it (messages #1, #2, #3), and no external caller was reported. The one residual cost, out-of-tree breakage, is a compatibility question for another angle.
